title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
text:
This exercise moves on from mapping points to actually testing whether a set of points is clustered, dispersed, or effectively random. We reuse two files from Hands-on Exercise 1: PreSchoolsLocation.geojson (the points we’re testing) and MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson (used here as the study area boundary rather than an administrative map).
The new package is spatstat, which does point pattern analysis. It expects its own ppp (planar point pattern) object rather than an sf object, so a chunk of this exercise is just converting formats.

pacman::p_load(sf, spatstat, tmap, tidyverse)

The original textbook uses a dedicated coastal outline shapefile as the study area. We don’t have that file, so instead we dissolve all the subzone polygons into one single outline with st_union(). It’s a reasonable stand-in: the result is still “all of Singapore’s land area,” just derived a different way.

sg_sf <- mpsz %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_sf()

plot(st_geometry(sg_sf))

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Converting to spatstat’s ppp format
spatstat needs a planar point pattern (ppp) plus an observation window (owin). The window comes from the dissolved outline; the points come from the preschool coordinates.
The dissolved outline inherits every vertex from the original 323 subzone polygons, which makes for a very detailed coastline (thousands of points). That level of detail isn’t actually needed just to define a study-area boundary, and it makes the distance-based calculations later in this exercise (especially the F-function envelope) extremely slow. So the window gets simplified first, with a small tolerance that doesn’t visibly change the shape at Singapore’s scale.

sg_sf_simplified <- sg_sf %>%
  st_simplify(dTolerance = 20, preserveTopology = TRUE)

sg_owin <- as.owin(sg_sf_simplified)

preschool_ppp <- as.ppp(st_coordinates(preschool), W = sg_owin)

plot(preschool_ppp)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
section: Part 1 — First-order analysis: where are preschools concentrated?
text:
Part 1 — First-order analysis: where are preschools concentrated?
First-order analysis asks a simple question: where is the density of points higher or lower across the study area? The tool for this is kernel density estimation (KDE) — instead of looking at exact points, we smear each point out into a little “bump” and add all the bumps up into a continuous surface.

Fixed bandwidth
sigma controls how wide that bump is (the bandwidth). A fixed value is the simplest starting point.

kde_fixed <- density(preschool_ppp_jit,
                      sigma = 500,
                      edge = TRUE,
                      kernel = "gaussian")
plot(kde_fixed, main = "Fixed bandwidth (sigma = 500m)")










Automatic bandwidth selection
Picking sigma by eye is a bit arbitrary. spatstat has a few automatic selectors that pick a bandwidth based on the data itself:

bw.diggle(preschool_ppp_jit)

   sigma 
270.1161 

bw.CvL(preschool_ppp_jit)

   sigma 
6471.187 

bw.scott(preschool_ppp_jit)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2111.808 1347.555 

bw.ppl(preschool_ppp_jit)

   sigma 
156.8283 


These rarely agree exactly — they’re optimising for different things (bw.diggle for detecting clusters, bw.CvL and bw.scott more for a smooth overall estimate). Worth plotting a couple of them side by side to see how much the choice actually changes the picture:

kde_diggle <- density(preschool_ppp_jit, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
kde_ppl <- density(preschool_ppp_jit, sigma = bw.ppl, edge = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_diggle, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Clark-Evans test
KDE gives a picture; the Clark-Evans test gives a number and a p-value. It compares the average distance between each point and its nearest neighbour to what we’d expect under complete spatial randomness (CSR). A ratio below 1 suggests clustering, above 1 suggests a more even/dispersed spread.

clarkevans.test(preschool_ppp_jit,
                 correction = "none",
                 clipregion = sg_owin,
                 alternative = "clustered",
                 nsim = 99)

    No edge correction

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
section: Part 2 — Second-order analysis: is the clustering statistically real?
text:
Part 2 — Second-order analysis: is the clustering statistically real?
First-order analysis describes the overall density surface but doesn’t really tell us whether an apparent cluster is meaningful or just noise. Second-order analysis looks at pairs of points and asks whether, at a given distance, points tend to have more or fewer neighbours than a random pattern would.
The general approach for all four functions below is the same: compute the observed statistic, then simulate many random point patterns (Monte Carlo) inside the same window and see whether the observed line sits outside the range the random simulations produce.

G-function — nearest neighbour distance

G <- Gest(preschool_ppp_jit)
plot(G, main = "G-function")









G.csr <- envelope(preschool_ppp_jit, Gest, nsim = 39)

plot(F, main = "F-function")









F.csr <- envelope(preschool_ppp_jit, Fest, nsim = 39)

plot(F.csr, main = "F-function vs CSR envelope")










K-function — points within a given radius
Unlike G and F, the K-function looks at every pair of points, which is inherently a heavier computation. By default spatstat also applies isotropic edge correction, which involves extra geometric work against the window boundary and gets noticeably slow on a window made up of many separate pieces (Singapore’s mainland plus its various small islands). Border correction is a simpler, much faster alternative that still gives a valid estimate, so it’s used explicitly here.

K <- Kest(preschool_ppp_jit, correction = "border")
plot(K, . - r ~ r, main = "K-function")









K.csr <- envelope(preschool_ppp_jit, Kest, nsim = 39, correction = "border")

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Reading the envelope plots
For all four functions, the grey band is the range produced by 99 simulations of a completely random pattern in the same window. If the observed (black) line climbs above the grey band, points are more clustered than random at that distance; if it drops below, they’re more dispersed than random; if it stays inside the band, we can’t tell the pattern apart from CSR at that scale.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Point Pattern Analysis
text:
Notes and open questions
This exercise reuses Hands-on Ex01’s preschool and subzone data rather than the childcare-centre dataset the textbook chapter uses, and substitutes a dissolved subzone outline for the missing coastal-outline shapefile — worth stating plainly rather than pretending it’s the original dataset. A natural next step, if time allows, is repeating the analysis on a single planning area rather than the whole island, since CSR across all of Singapore is a fairly blunt test — preschool placement almost certainly depends on where people live, not on land area alone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
The goal of this exercise is to get familiar with sf (simple features), R’s core package for handling geospatial data. Specifically, we will:

Set up an R environment for geospatial analysis.
Import three different geospatial data formats: GeoJSON (polygons), KML (points), and ESRI Shapefile (lines).
Import a plain tabular dataset with latitude/longitude columns and convert it into a spatial layer.
Inspect the data and assign/transform its coordinate reference system (CRS).
Run basic GIS geoprocessing: buffering and point-in-polygon counting.
Use ggplot2 for exploratory data analysis (EDA).

Coming from Python, a few of the R equivalents I kept looking up: geopandas.read_file() is sf::st_read(), a GeoDataFrame is basically an sf object (a data frame with an extra geometry column), gdf.crs/gdf.to_crs() map to st_crs()/st_transform(), gdf.buffer(5) is st_buffer(x, dist = 5), and the %>% pipe does roughly what method chaining does in pandas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
2.1 Packages used

sf: reads/writes geospatial data and handles geometric operations and coordinate systems.
tidyverse: a collection of data-wrangling packages, including readr (read CSV), dplyr (data manipulation), ggplot2 (plotting), etc.
rvest: HTML parsing. Some GeoJSON exports from data.gov.sg pack all attribute fields into a single HTML table, so this is needed to pull them out.

Using pacman::p_load() instead of install.packages() + library() — it installs a package if it’s missing and just loads it otherwise, so it’s one line instead of two.

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, rvest)

This one only has Name and Description — the actual name, code, etc. are packed into an HTML table inside Description. Since this exercise only needs the pre-schools’ geometry to do a point-in-polygon count and never touches the name/code fields, I skipped parsing that out and went straight to the analysis below.
If I wanted CENTRE_NAME later (e.g. to label pre-schools on a map), the same rvest approach used in Hands-on Exercise 2 would work here too:
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  page  <- read_html(html_text)
  rows  <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

preschool <- preschool %>%
  mutate(CENTRE_NAME = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "CENTRE_NAME")) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

text:
5.2 Assigning vs. transforming CRS
st_set_crs() and st_transform() do very different things despite sounding similar. st_set_crs() just applies a label — it tells R “this data was already in this CRS”, without touching the coordinate values. Use it when a file’s CRS is missing or mislabelled. st_transform() actually re-projects the data, recalculating the coordinates — use it when the current CRS is known and correct, and the goal is to convert to a different one.
GeoJSON and KML are WGS84 (EPSG:4326) by convention, so st_transform() is the right call here:

mpsz3414      <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)
preschool3414 <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

The cycling path Shapefile is usually already in SVY21, but its .prj file often doesn’t encode the EPSG code correctly (st_crs() may show NA or 9001 for the EPSG). In that case it just needs the correct label applied:

# if st_crs(cyclingpath) above shows an EPSG other than 3414, run this to apply the correct label
cyclingpath3414 <- st_set_crs(cyclingpath, 3414)

st_crs(cyclingpath3414)$epsg

[1] 3414


A quick way to tell which function is needed: look at the coordinate values. Small decimals like 103.8, 1.35 are lat/long, so st_transform(); six-digit numbers like 28000, 33000 are already SVY21, so just st_set_crs() to label it.
Confirm the three layers line up:

plot(st_geometry(mpsz3414))
plot(st_geometry(preschool3414), add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 20, cex = 0.3)

7.1 Scenario 1: Land area needed to widen the cycling paths
Suppose the government wants to widen every existing cycling path by 5 metres on each side — how much land would need to be acquired?
Step 1: Create a 5-metre buffer.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath3414,
  dist = 5,        # units are metres (since the CRS is 3414)
  nQuadSegs = 30   # 30 line segments approximate each quarter-circle — higher means smoother corners
)

Step 2: Calculate the area of each buffer polygon and add it as a column.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

Step 3: Sum up the total area.

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

  units::set_units(km^2)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
A thematic map uses symbols, colour, or texture to show the spatial distribution of a geographic phenomenon — population density, rainfall, poverty rate, and so on. The goal of this exercise is to use the tmap package to draw a choropleth map of the dependency ratio for each planning subzone in Singapore, based on 2024 population data.
We’ll cover:

Import the 2019 subzone boundary and, where needed, use rvest to extract attribute fields from the HTML table embedded in Description.
Wrangle the 2024 population table: compute the YOUNG / ECONOMY ACTIVE / AGED age bands and the dependency ratio.
Use left_join() to attach the population data to the geographic layer, and save an RDS backup.
Build up maps with tmap, from simple to advanced: quick mapping → layer stacking → classification & colour → cartographic decorations → small multiples → statistical charts → interactive maps.

One thing worth noting up front: tmap went through a fairly large syntax overhaul in version 4, so v3-style code (which is what most older blog posts and Stack Overflow answers still use) will error or throw deprecation warnings here. The renames that tripped me up most: tm_polygons(col = "VAR") is now tm_polygons(fill = "VAR"); style/palette arguments move into fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(...); legend titles move into fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "..."); tm_scale_bar() is now tm_scalebar(); and tm_layout(main.title = ...) is now tm_title(...). The rule I kept repeating to myself: fill is always the polygon’s fill colour, col is always a line/border colour.

For reference, here’s what the KML route would have looked like. Reading the KML in only gives Name and Description, with the attributes packed into an HTML table inside Description:
mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)   # KML is WGS84, transform to Singapore's SVY21 (EPSG:3414)

The HTML inside Description is a table, where each <tr> row is a <th> (field name) paired with a <td> (field value):
# given an HTML string and a field name, return that field's value
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  page  <- read_html(html_text)          # parse into an HTML document object
  rows  <- page %>% html_elements("tr")  # get all <tr> rows
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%  # keep the row whose th matches the target field
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N   = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N  = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C  = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())
And a faster version that parses each record once instead of once per field:
parse_kml_desc <- function(html_text) {
  rows <- read_html(html_text) %>% html_elements("tr")
  keys <- rows %>% html_element("th") %>% html_text2()
  vals <- rows %>% html_element("td") %>% html_text2()
  ok <- !is.na(keys) & !is.na(vals)
  as_tibble(setNames(as.list(vals[ok]), keys[ok]))
}

attrs <- map_dfr(mpsz$Description, parse_kml_desc)
mpsz <- bind_cols(st_drop_geometry(mpsz), attrs) %>%

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
4.1 Goal
Turn the long-format table (one row per age group × sex × dwelling type) into a wide format (one row per subzone), producing three age-band columns:

YOUNG: ages 0–24
ECONOMY ACTIVE: ages 25–64
AGED: ages 65+
DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY ACTIVE

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
section: 4.2 Group by the lower bound of each age band
text:
4.2 Group by the lower bound of each age band
The AG column looks like 0_to_4, 25_to_29, 90_and_over. A regular expression pulls out the leading number as the age band’s lower bound, then buckets it into one of the three groups.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  # extract the leading number from AG, e.g. "25_to_29" -> 25, "90_and_over" -> 90
  mutate(AGE_LOWER = as.numeric(str_extract(AG, "^\\d+"))) %>%
  mutate(AGE_GROUP = case_when(
    AGE_LOWER < 25 ~ "YOUNG",
    AGE_LOWER < 65 ~ "ECONOMY ACTIVE",
    TRUE           ~ "AGED"
  )) %>%
  # sum population within the same subzone and age band (across sex and dwelling type)
  group_by(PA, SZ, AGE_GROUP) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # pivot long to wide: each of the three AGE_GROUP values becomes its own column
  pivot_wider(names_from = AGE_GROUP, values_from = POP, values_fill = 0) %>%
  # compute total population and the dependency ratio
  mutate(
    TOTAL      = YOUNG + `ECONOMY ACTIVE` + AGED,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)

head(popdata2024)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  PA         SZ                    YOUNG `ECONOMY ACTIVE`  AGED TOTAL DEPENDENCY
  <chr>      <chr>                 <dbl>            <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Ang Mo Kio Ang Mo Kio Town Cent…  1220             2750   900  4870      0.771
2 Ang Mo Kio Cheng San              4960            15240  6810 27010      0.772
3 Ang Mo Kio Chong Boon             4300            13560  6850 24710      0.822
4 Ang Mo Kio Kebun Bahru            4130            12070  5650 21850      0.810
5 Ang Mo Kio Sembawang Hills        1840             3570  1430  6840      0.916
6 Ang Mo Kio Shangri-la             3720             9400  4210 17330      0.844


ECONOMY ACTIVE has a space in it, so it needs backticks every time it’s referenced in R — `ECONOMY ACTIVE` — which is why the code above has so many of them.
For reference, the course material actually sums columns by position instead of by name (after pivot_wider, columns land in alphabetical order, so 5_to_9 ends up after 45_to_49, which is why the index ranges look scattered):
popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) + rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)
Both give the same numbers, but I went with the name-based version — the positional one would quietly compute the wrong answer if the data version changes or the number of age groups shifts, since it’s just trusting that column 3 is still whatever it was before.

4.3 Handling case and edge cases
The geographic layer’s SUBZONE_N is all uppercase (MARINA SOUTH), while the population table’s SZ is title case (Marina South) — the join won’t match unless these are unified. Also filtered out subzones with a zero denominator, which would otherwise produce Inf in the ratio.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%   # convert PA and SZ to all-uppercase
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)             # avoid Inf in the dependency ratio

4.5 Export an RDS backup
RDS is R’s native binary format and fully preserves an sf object’s class and CRS, so this saves having to re-run the whole preprocessing pipeline next time.

# create the rds folder if it doesn't exist
if (!dir.exists("data/rds")) dir.create("data/rds", recursive = TRUE)

write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

To reload it later:

mpsz_pop2024 <- read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
5.1 Quick mapping: qtm()
qtm() is short for “quick thematic map” — one line, good for a first look while exploring.

tmap_mode("plot")   # "plot" = static map; "view" = interactive map
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, fill = "DEPENDENCY")








It’s not really customisable though, so the layer-stacking syntax below is what actually gets used for the real output.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
5.2 tmap’s layer grammar
Like ggplot2, tmap stacks layers with +:
tm_shape(data) +        # first declare which spatial data to draw
  tm_polygons(...) +    # then decide how to draw it (fill, borders...)
  tm_compass() + ...    # finally add cartographic decorations

5.2.1 A blank base map

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()










5.2.2 Adding a fill variable

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")










5.2.3 Controlling tm_fill() and tm_borders() separately
tm_polygons() is really tm_fill() + tm_borders() combined — splitting them lets fill and border be controlled independently.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Customising the border style:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",     # border colour
             lwd = 0.1,          # line width
             lty = "dashed")     # line type

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
6.1 Quantile
Each class gets the same number of subzones, so every colour on the map ends up used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
6.2 Equal
Splits the value range into n equally-sized intervals — on skewed data, most subzones can end up crammed into a single colour.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Comparing the two on the same data: quantile spreads colours out evenly, which makes ranking easy to read; equal reflects the actual spacing between values more faithfully. Neither is objectively “correct” — the classification method chosen actually shapes how a reader interprets the map, so it’s worth picking on purpose rather than just leaving the default. (tm_scale_intervals() also supports style = "jenks" for natural breaks, "sd" for standard deviation, "pretty" for round-number breaks, and a few others.)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
6.3 Custom Breaks
Checking the summary statistics first helps pick sensible cut points:

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6632  0.7254  0.7021  0.8051  1.0940     100 



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








breaks needs n+1 values (min and max included) and has to cover the full range of the data, otherwise anything outside that range shows up grey as a missing value.

text:
8.1 Legend
In v4, legend settings live under the matching aesthetic’s .legend argument — fill.legend = tm_legend(...).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio",
                position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
                frame = TRUE)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
8.2 Compass, scale bar, and grid

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +           # compass
  tm_scalebar() +                                   # scale bar
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +                 # lat/long grid
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from URA\nand Population data from DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))        # data-source credit








A few naming things worth remembering here: tm_compass(type = ...) takes "arrow", "4star", "8star", "radar", or "rose"; v4 uses tm_scalebar() with no underscore (v3’s tm_scale_bar() is deprecated); and tm_title() replaces v3’s tm_layout(main.title = ...).

text:
9.3 Method 3: tm_facets() (facet by a categorical column)
One small map per region, based on REGION_N.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, ncols = 3,
            free.coords = TRUE,    # let each small map zoom to its own extent
            drop.units = TRUE) +   # don't draw subzones that don't belong to that facet
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",

10.1 Attaching a boxplot next to the map
fill.chart, new in v4, attaches a distribution chart directly next to the legend.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +   # add a boxplot
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

text:
10.2 Flagging outliers
The boxplot shows there are outliers, but not where they are on the map. boxplot.stats() finds them, then a red outline marks them.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats        <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)  # the returned $out is the set of outliers
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf   <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

outlier_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, DEPENDENCY)

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +

  # stack a second layer: a red outline and label for the outlier subzones

Worth noting how the layering works here: tm_shape() can appear more than once in the same call, and each time it does, everything after it switches to that new data source. That’s how the red outline layer above only applies to outlier_sf and not the whole map.

  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +

# otherwise every map after this becomes interactive, bloating the site and slowing rendering
tmap_mode("plot")

Every interactive map bundles Leaflet’s JS/CSS into the page, which adds up fast — I kept it to just this one interactive map in the whole document and used static maps everywhere else so the site doesn’t get too heavy.
